title: What's this?
goal: Point at the things around you, name them, make plurals — and meet vowel harmony, the law that governs this whole language.
bekal: tell *bu*, *şu* and *o* apart by distance from the speaker
read the last vowel of a word and predict the shape of the ending that will attach to it
make plurals with *-ler* or *-lar* without ever picking the wrong one

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Yeni oda
dialogs.intro: Ayşe takes Budi to his rented room in Kadıköy and shows him what's in it, one thing at a time.

lines.speaker: Ayşe:
lines.id: Here's the room. Do you like it?

lines.speaker: Ayşe:
lines.text: O bir dolap. Şu da masa.
lines.id: That's a wardrobe. And that one's a table.
lines.literal: that a wardrobe. that-there too table.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Masa mı? Bizde "masa" başka bir şey!
lines.id: A table? Back home "masa" is something else!
lines.literal: table question? us-at "masa" other a thing!

lines.speaker: Ayşe:
lines.text: Öyle mi? Peki bunlar ne, biliyor musunuz?
lines.id: Really? Well, do you know what these are?
lines.literal: so question? well these what, knowing are-you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Books and notebooks. These I know!

lines.speaker: Ayşe:
lines.text: O ev sahibi, Fatma Hanım. Çok iyi bir insan.
lines.id: That's the landlady, Ms. Fatma. A very kind person.
lines.literal: she house owner-its, Fatma Ms. very good a person.

lines.speaker: Ayşe:
lines.id: In the door. Here are the keys.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Thank you, Ms. Ayşe. You're very kind.

notes: **Turkish has no obligatory "a".** *Dolap* already means "wardrobe" or "a wardrobe". The word *bir* (one) can be used like "a", but it adds a sense of "some, one or other": *bir kadın* = "a woman (someone I don't know)".

**No "the" either.** If you want to say "THAT book, the one we just talked about", Turkish marks it not in front of the word but with the object ending *-i* after it. That's for Unit 9 — for now just know the marker exists, and that it goes at the end.

**Bunları, not bunlar.** In the dialogue, *Bunları biliyorum* has an extra *-ı* because the things are the target of the verb "know". Don't memorize this now; just notice that the same word changes its tail depending on its job in the sentence.

**Aferin** is used to praise children, students, or anyone who has just managed something — just like "well done!" or "good job!". To praise an adult for something serious, use *helal olsun* or *bravo*.

sections.title: Vowel harmony — the one law of Turkish

blocks.text: If you could remember only one page of this entire course, pick this one. Turkish endings have no fixed form: they **adapt to the last vowel of the word they attach to**. That's why "in/at" can appear as *-de*, *-da*, *-te* or *-ta* — and all four are the same ending.
Turkish's eight vowels split in two by tongue position. **Back** vowels: *a, ı, o, u*. **Front** vowels: *e, i, ö, ü*. The rule: an ending follows the group of the last vowel of its host word.

blocks.title: Use it in your head, not from the table
items: Don't memorize the table. Practice one habit: every time you meet a new word, say its last vowel out loud. *Kitap* → **a**. *Deniz* → **i**. *Okul* → **u**. *Göz* → **ö**.
After that, the ending simply follows. The matching vowel will feel comfortable in your mouth, the wrong one will feel awkward — and after a few weeks, your ear decides, not the table.
Loanwords occasionally rebel: *saat* → *saatler* (not *saatlar*), *kalp* → *kalbim*. There are only a few, and this course flags them every time they come up.

blocks.text: *O* does double duty: besides "that", it also means "he/she/it". *O öğretmen* can mean "he/she is a teacher" or "that teacher" — context decides, and in practice it almost never causes confusion.
*Şu* has a special flavor: it points to something that **has just entered the conversation**, often while pointing with your hand. If you're unsure between *şu* and *o*, use *o*.

blocks.title: When the plural is not used
items: After a number, the noun STAYS singular: *üç kitap* (three books), not *üç kitaplar*. The number already makes it plural, so *-lar* is redundant — and sounds wrong to a Turkish ear.
The same goes after *çok* (many) and *birkaç* (a few): *çok insan*, *birkaç gün*.

blocks.text: *Bilgisayar* is one of the modern Turkish words that were coined, not borrowed: *bilgi* (information) + *saymak* (to count) — "information counter". Turkish has an institution that busily mints words like this, and some of them really catch on.

blocks.title: Unit 1 review
items: Cover Unit 1, then rebuild the Turkish sentences from memory: "My name is Budi." · "I'm from Indonesia." · "How are you, ma'am?" · "I'm not a teacher." · "See you!"
If three out of five come out without stopping to think, you can move on.
